hitler-kanzler.text: Adolf Hitler becomes Reich Chancellor. The National Socialists set up a dictatorship.

pogrom.text: National Socialists and their followers destroy synagogues and Jewish shops.

kriegsbeginn.text: The Second World War begins. It lasts until 1945.

stauffenberg.text: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg tries to kill Hitler. The attempt fails.

auschwitz.text: The Auschwitz extermination camp is liberated. Today 27 January is the day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism.

kriegsende.text: Germany surrenders unconditionally. The war in Europe is over.

besatzungszonen.text: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France divide Germany into four zones and Berlin into four sectors.

luftbruecke.text: The Soviet Union blocks all land routes to West Berlin. Aircraft supply the city for almost a year.

brd-gruendung.text: The Federal Republic of Germany is founded in the three western zones. Konrad Adenauer becomes the first Federal Chancellor.

ddr-gruendung.text: The German Democratic Republic is founded in the Soviet zone.

wirtschaftswunder.text: The economy of the Federal Republic grows very fast.

gastarbeiter.text: The Federal Republic recruits workers from abroad. The first come from Italy.

volksaufstand.text: Strikes and a popular uprising across the GDR. It is put down by force.

roemische-vertraege.text: The Federal Republic and five other states found the European Economic Community (EEC).

mauerbau.text: The GDR builds the Wall. Berlin stays divided until 1989.

kniefall.text: Federal Chancellor Willy Brandt kneels in Warsaw and asks Poland and the Polish Jews for forgiveness. His Eastern Treaties ease relations with the East.

montagsdemos.text: People in the GDR demonstrate peacefully and call "Wir sind das Volk". The dictatorship comes to an end.

mauerfall.text: The Wall in Berlin is opened for everyone.

einheit.text: The five eastern states join the Federal Republic. Germany is one state again, in the borders of today.

euro.text: People in Germany pay with euro notes and coins.

places.berlin-sectors: Berlin: four sectors, in the middle of the Soviet zone

symbole.title: Name, flag, anthem and eagle
symbole.big: Germany's name, flag, anthem and eagle are the signs of the democratic state that was founded in 1949.

name.body: The full name is {{Bundesrepublik Deutschland}}. {{Bund}} means federation: 16 states together form one country. {{Republik}} means a state without a king or queen. So the name already says how Germany is built.
name.front: What is the full name of Germany?
name.note: Bund: a federation of states. Republik: no monarch.

falle-bundes.text: The wrong options also begin with {{Bundes}}: {{Bundesstaat Deutschland}}, {{Bundesländer Deutschland}}, {{Bundesbezirk Deutschland}}. Germany **is** a {{Bundesstaat}} (a federal state), but its name is {{Bundesrepublik Deutschland}}.

einwohner.q: How many people live in Germany?
einwohner.body: About 84 million people live in Germany. The other options are 70, 78 and 90 million. Remember it as a little more than 80 million.
einwohner.front: How many inhabitants does Germany have?

flagge.q: Which colours does the German flag have?
flagge.body: The flag has three stripes: {{schwarz-rot-gold}}, from top to bottom. In German the third colour is called {{gold}}, not yellow ({{gelb}}). The wrong options change one colour or the order.
flagge.front: The colours of the German flag, from top to bottom?
flagge.note: The third colour is gold, never gelb.

hymne.q: How does the national anthem begin?
hymne.body: The national anthem begins with the words {{Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit}}. That means: unity and justice and freedom. These three words name what the democratic state stands for.
hymne.front: The first words of the German national anthem?

adler.body: The heraldic animal ({{Wappentier}}) of Germany is the eagle ({{Adler}}). The coat of arms ({{Wappen}}) shows a black eagle on a golden shield. A large eagle, the {{Bundesadler}}, hangs in the plenary chamber of the {{Bundestag}}, the German parliament.
adler.front: Which animal is on Germany's coat of arms, and where does a large one hang?
adler.back: the eagle (Federal Eagle), in the plenary chamber of the Bundestag

wappen.caption: Picture 1 is the coat of arms of the Federal Republic: the black eagle on gold. Picture 4, with hammer and compass, is the coat of arms of the GDR.

plenarsaal.caption: The plenary chamber of the {{Bundestag}}. The large eagle on the wall is the {{Bundesadler}}.

falle-reich.text: {{Reichsadler}} and {{Reichskrone}} sound right but are wrong. {{Reich}} is the word for earlier German states. Today's state is the {{Bund}}, so its eagle is the {{Bundesadler}}.

items.q: What do the two parts of the name {{Bundesrepublik}} tell you?
items.a: {{Bund}}: several states form one federation. {{Republik}}: there is no king or queen.

items.q: Name the three colours of the flag in German, from the top.
items.a: {{schwarz}}, {{rot}}, {{gold}}

items.q: Why is the eagle in the {{Bundestag}} called {{Bundesadler}} and not {{Reichsadler}}?
items.a: Because today's state is the {{Bund}}, the federation. {{Reich}} is the word for earlier German states.

items.q: Which three words begin the national anthem?
items.a: {{Einigkeit}}, {{Recht}}, {{Freiheit}}: unity, justice, freedom.

wuerde.title: Human dignity comes first
wuerde.big: The Basic Law of 1949 is the answer to the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945: dignity comes first, and rights stay safe.

wuerde.q: Which fundamental right is in Article 1 of the Basic Law?
wuerde.body: Article 1 of the {{Grundgesetz}} (Basic Law) says: {{Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar}}. {{Unantastbar}} means inviolable: nobody may touch it. The state must respect and protect human dignity. In the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945 this was not so. The Basic Law of 1949 is the answer to that, so dignity comes first.
wuerde.front: What comes first in the Basic Law, in Article 1?
wuerde.note: The answer to the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945.

falle-rechte.text: The wrong options, {{Recht auf Leben}}, {{Religionsfreiheit}} and {{Meinungsfreiheit}}, are real fundamental rights too. But only human dignity comes **first**, in Article 1.

gleich-gesetz.q: What does the Basic Law say about equality?
gleich-gesetz.body: The Basic Law says: {{Alle sind vor dem Gesetz gleich}}. Everyone has the same rights, and the state may not treat its citizens ({{Bürgerinnen und Bürger}}) unequally. Equal rights do **not** mean equal money. The Basic Law never says that everyone should have the same amount of money. Freedom of expression, petitions ({{Petitionen}}, written requests to the authorities) and freedom of assembly are not forbidden: they are rights.
gleich-gesetz.front: What is the rule of the Basic Law about equality?
gleich-gesetz.back: Everyone is equal before the law.

zwangsarbeit.q: Which kind of work does the Basic Law forbid?
zwangsarbeit.body: The Basic Law forbids {{Zwangsarbeit}}: {{Zwang}} means force and {{Arbeit}} means work. Forced labour treats a person like a thing, and that hurts human dignity. The other options are not forbidden: {{Militärdienst}} (military service), {{freie Berufswahl}} (free choice of occupation) and {{Arbeit im Ausland}} (working abroad).
zwangsarbeit.front: Which kind of work is forbidden by the Basic Law?
zwangsarbeit.note: Zwang means force. It hurts dignity.

strafe.q: Which punishment is compatible with the Basic Law?
strafe.body: A punishment must respect human dignity. The {{Prügelstrafe}} (corporal punishment), {{Folter}} (torture) and {{Todesstrafe}} (death penalty) hurt or destroy a person. So the Basic Law does not allow them, and it abolished the death penalty in 1949. A {{Geldstrafe}} is compatible: {{Geld}} is money, and the person pays a fine. Body and life are not touched.
strafe.front: Which punishment does the Basic Law allow?
strafe.note: Beating, torture and the death penalty hurt dignity.

grundrecht-fest.q: Can a party abolish freedom of the press?
grundrecht-fest.body: No. {{Pressefreiheit}} (freedom of the press) is a {{Grundrecht}}, a fundamental right. A fundamental right cannot be abolished: not by a party, not by a majority in the {{Bundestag}} and not by the {{Bundesrat}}. The dictatorship of 1933 to 1945 took rights away from people. So the Basic Law of 1949 makes them safe.
grundrecht-fest.front: Can a party or a majority abolish a fundamental right?
grundrecht-fest.back: No, a fundamental right cannot be abolished.
grundrecht-fest.note: Freedom of the press is one of them.

falle-mehrheit.text: The wrong options name a simple majority, two thirds, or only the {{Bundesrat}}. All three are wrong. For a fundamental right, the number of votes does not matter.

items.q: Why does the Basic Law of 1949 start with human dignity?
items.a: It is the answer to the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945, in which dignity was not respected. Dignity must come first.

items.q: Why can no party and no majority abolish freedom of the press?
items.a: It is a {{Grundrecht}}, and fundamental rights cannot be abolished. The dictatorship of 1933 to 1945 took rights away, so the Basic Law protects them.

items.q: Name three punishments the Basic Law does not allow, and one that fits.
items.a: Not allowed: {{Prügelstrafe}}, {{Folter}}, {{Todesstrafe}}. Compatible: {{Geldstrafe}}.

items.q: Does {{Alle sind vor dem Gesetz gleich}} mean that everyone has the same amount of money?
items.a: No. It means equal rights. The Basic Law never promises equal money.

freiheiten.title: The freedoms of the Basic Law
freiheiten.big: The Basic Law guarantees freedoms such as opinion, faith, movement and assembly; asylum is the one fundamental right only for foreigners.

meinung.q: Why may people in Germany speak out against the government?
meinung.body: The reason is {{Meinungsfreiheit}} (freedom of expression), not taxes and not the right to vote. {{Meinung}} means opinion. Everyone may say openly what they think, also against the government and also on the internet. It is one of the fundamental rights ({{Grundrechte}}). Nobody has to agree with the government first.
meinung.case: Someone writes a post on the internet against the government. That is allowed.
meinung.front: Which freedom lets you criticise the government openly?
meinung.note: It is a fundamental right. It counts on the internet too.

falle-faust.text: {{Faustrecht}} (the law of the fist), {{Selbstjustiz}} (taking the law into your own hands) and {{Waffenbesitz}} (owning weapons) are not fundamental rights. In Germany courts and police enforce the law, not private persons.

meinung-grenze.q: Where does freedom of expression end?
meinung-grenze.body: Freedom of expression has limits, because other people have rights too. It ends where someone spreads false claims ({{falsche Behauptungen}}) about individual people in public. Insulting people is not covered, and Nazi, Hamas or Islamic State symbols may not be shown in public. Opinions about the government, criticism of the state and discussions about religions are **not** a limit. They are allowed.
meinung-grenze.front: Where does freedom of expression end in Germany?
meinung-grenze.back: when false claims about individual people are spread in public
meinung-grenze.note: Criticism of the state is allowed.

glaube.q: What do freedom of faith and conscience protect?
glaube.body: {{Glaube}} means faith and {{Gewissen}} means conscience, the inner sense of right and wrong. Everyone may choose a religion, change it or have none. The state may not force a faith on anyone. This is a fundamental right. A right to work, housing or entertainment is not one.
glaube.front: Which freedom lets you choose your religion, or none?
glaube.note: Work, housing, entertainment: not fundamental rights.

religionsunterricht.q: Who decides about religious education until age 14?
religionsunterricht.body: Faith is a personal choice. So until a child is 14, the parents decide whether it goes to {{Religionsunterricht}} (religious education) at school. {{Unterricht}} means lesson. History, civics and language lessons are regular school subjects: the parents do not decide about them. From 14, the young person decides alone about their faith.
religionsunterricht.front: Which school subject can parents choose for a child until 14?
religionsunterricht.note: From 14, the young person decides about faith.

freizuegigkeit.q: What does the right of freedom of movement mean?
freizuegigkeit.body: {{Freizügigkeit}} means that you may choose where you live. You can move from one city or state to another. The word contains {{frei}} (free) and {{ziehen}} (to move to a new place). Changing your job and changing your religion are different rights.
freizuegigkeit.front: Which right do you use when you choose a new home town?
freizuegigkeit.back: Freedom of movement: you may choose where you live.

demo.q: What must you do before a demonstration in the street?
demo.body: {{Versammlungsfreiheit}} is the right to meet with others peacefully and to demonstrate. A demonstration in the street must be registered ({{anmelden}}) with the authorities beforehand. Anyone can register one: you do not need to found an association ({{Verein}}). Demonstrations are allowed, but not anywhere and at any time without registration.
demo.case: Maik and Sybille want to demonstrate with friends in their town. They register the demonstration first.
demo.front: What must you do first if you want to hold a demonstration?
demo.note: Anyone can register: no association needed.

briefgeheimnis.q: What right do you break if you open someone else's letter?
briefgeheimnis.body: A letter belongs to the person it is addressed to. {{Brief}} means letter and {{Geheimnis}} means secret. The {{Briefgeheimnis}} says that nobody else may open it. If you open another person's letter on purpose, you do not respect this right.
briefgeheimnis.front: What right do you break by opening a letter for someone else?

falle-schweigen.text: {{Schweigerecht}} is the right to stay silent, for example when the police ask questions. {{Schweigepflicht}} is the duty to keep a secret, for example for a doctor. Both are about silence, not about letters.

asyl.q: Which fundamental right is only for foreigners?
asyl.body: {{Asyl}} (asylum) is the one fundamental right that applies only to foreigners ({{Ausländerinnen/Ausländer}}). It protects people who are persecuted for political reasons in their own country. They come from abroad, so the right belongs to foreigners only. Human dignity, protection of the family and freedom of expression apply to everyone.
asyl.front: Which fundamental right protects people persecuted for political reasons?
asyl.note: The only fundamental right just for foreigners.

items.q: Why may people criticise the government, and where does this freedom end?
items.a: {{Meinungsfreiheit}} allows it. It ends at false claims about individual people, spread in public.

items.q: Which freedom do you use to choose a new home town, and which to choose a religion?
items.a: {{Freizügigkeit}} for the home town. {{Glaubens- und Gewissensfreiheit}} for the religion.

items.q: Two friends plan a demonstration in the street: what must they do first?
items.a: They must register it ({{anmelden}}). They do not need an association.

items.q: Which fundamental right is only for foreigners, and who does it protect?
items.a: {{Asyl}}. It protects people who are persecuted for political reasons in their own country.

gleichbehandlung.title: Equal treatment and discrimination
gleichbehandlung.big: Nobody may be treated worse because of who they are, such as a disability or skin colour, at work or in public.

gleichbehandlung.q: What does equal treatment mean in Germany?
gleichbehandlung.body: {{Gleich}} means equal and {{behandeln}} means to treat. Nobody may be treated worse ({{benachteiligen}}) because of who they are, for example because of a disability. A personal reason, such as dislike, is **never** enough. A person who is disadvantaged may go to court ({{klagen}}). Every person has the same dignity, so nobody is worth less.
gleichbehandlung.front: What is the rule of equal treatment, with one example?
gleichbehandlung.back: Nobody may be disadvantaged, for example because of a disability.
gleichbehandlung.note: Personal dislike is never a reason.

bewerbung.q: When is rejecting a job applicant discrimination?
bewerbung.body: Discrimination ({{Diskriminierung}}) is when someone is treated worse only because of who they are. An employer may look at experience, languages and salary expectations ({{Gehaltsvorstellungen}}). These belong to the job. Being a mother ({{Mutter}}), sitting in a wheelchair ({{Rollstuhl}}) or having dark skin has nothing to do with it.
bewerbung.front: When is a rejected job application discrimination?
bewerbung.back: when the only reason is being a mother, using a wheelchair or having dark skin

bewerbung-vergleich.title: Discrimination or a reason about the job?
head: Discrimination
Reason about the job
rows: No English, no experience, salary too high
No experience, salary too high, no English
German too weak, no experience, salary too high

falle-nur-deshalb.text: The question says {{nur deshalb}} (**only** because). Experience, languages and salary expectations are reasons about the job, so a wrong option names one of them. The right option names the person: mother, wheelchair, dark skin.

schwimmbad.q: Which right is violated when a public pool refuses people because of skin colour?
schwimmbad.body: Two friends with dark skin want to enter a public swimming pool ({{Schwimmbad}}). They are refused because of their skin colour. That is unequal treatment, so the right to {{Gleichbehandlung}} is violated. The other options are other freedoms: expression, assembly and movement. Equal treatment applies in public places as well as at work.
schwimmbad.front: Which right is violated if people are refused entry because of skin colour?

items.q: What does equal treatment mean, with one example?
items.a: Nobody may be treated worse because of who they are, for example because of a disability.

items.q: When is the rejection of a job applicant discrimination?
items.a: When the only reason is a personal trait: being a mother, a wheelchair, dark skin. Experience, languages or salary are not.

items.q: Two friends are refused at a public swimming pool because of their skin colour: which right is violated?
items.a: The right to {{Gleichbehandlung}}, equal treatment.

items.q: Why may nobody be treated worse because of who they are?
items.a: Every person has the same dignity, so nobody is worth less than another.

staatsform.title: What kind of state Germany is
staatsform.big: Germany is a republic and a democratic and social {{Bundesstaat}}, and its constitution is the {{Grundgesetz}}.

grundgesetz.body: The constitution of Germany is called the {{Grundgesetz}}. {{Grund}} means basis and {{Gesetz}} means law. It has been in force since 1949, and all other laws must agree with it. The wrong options sound similar, for example {{Bundesgesetz}}, {{Volksgesetz}} and {{Bundesverfassung}}, but none of them is the name.
grundgesetz.front: Which special name does the German constitution have?

republik.q: Is Germany a republic or a monarchy?
republik.body: Germany is a {{Republik}}: it has no king or queen, and the head of state is a president. The wrong options for this are {{Monarchie}}, {{Diktatur}} and {{Fürstentum}} (principality). Some questions ask what Germany is **not**. Then {{Demokratie}}, {{Rechtsstaat}} and {{Sozialstaat}} are all true. The one that is false is {{Monarchie}}.
republik.front: Which form of state is Germany, and which is it not?

bundesstaat.q: How is the German state built?
bundesstaat.body: Germany is a {{Bundesstaat}}: 16 states together form one country. Article 20 of the {{Grundgesetz}} calls Germany a {{demokratischer und sozialer Bundesstaat}}. {{Demokratisch}} means the people rule, and {{sozial}} means the state cares for people in need. {{Sozial}} is **not** the same as {{sozialistisch}}, and {{kommunistisch}} and {{kapitalistisch}} are wrong, too.
bundesstaat.front: What kind of state is Germany? Give the full description.
bundesstaat.back: a democratic and social federal state

staatsformen.title: One state or a union of states?
head: {{Bundesstaat}}
{{Staatenbund}}
{{Zentralstaat}}
rows: several states in a loose union
shared by the federation and the states

falle-verbund.text: {{Staatenverbund}} and {{Staatenbund}} look like {{Bundesstaat}}, but both name a union of several states. Germany is one state that consists of 16 states.

religion.q: How are state and religion related in Germany?
religion.body: In Germany, state and religious communities ({{Religionsgemeinschaften}}) are separate: {{getrennt}}. The state does not follow one religion, and no religious community rules the state. The wrong options use other words: {{bilden}} (form), {{abhängig}} (dependent) and {{Einheit}} (unity).
religion.front: How are state and religion related in Germany?
religion.back: State and religious communities are separate.

items.q: What does {{Grund}} in {{Grundgesetz}} tell you?
items.a: It is the basis. All other laws must agree with it.

items.q: Which of {{Demokratie}}, {{Monarchie}}, {{Rechtsstaat}} and {{Sozialstaat}} is Germany **not**?
items.a: {{Monarchie}}. Germany is a {{Republik}}, with no king or queen.

items.q: Why is Germany a {{Bundesstaat}} and not a {{Staatenbund}}?
items.a: It is one state made of 16 states, not a loose union of several states.

items.q: Which German word shows that state and religion are separate?
items.a: {{getrennt}}. The state does not depend on a religious community.

gewalten.title: The people and the three powers
gewalten.big: All state power comes from the people, and it is split into three powers so that nobody holds all of it.

volkssouveraenitaet.q: Where does state power come from in Germany?
volkssouveraenitaet.body: {{Volkssouveränität}} means that all state power ({{Staatsgewalt}}) comes from the people: {{vom Volke}}. The people use this power in elections, for example when they elect the {{Bundestag}}. It does not come from the {{Bundestag}}, from a king or queen, from the {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}} or from interest groups ({{Interessenverbände}}). A king who rules over the people is the opposite of {{Volkssouveränität}}.
volkssouveraenitaet.meaning: popular sovereignty: the people hold the power
volkssouveraenitaet.front: Where does all state power come from in a democracy?
volkssouveraenitaet.back: All state power comes from the people.
volkssouveraenitaet.note: Not a king, not the Bundestag.

gewaltenteilung.q: How is state power divided in Germany?
gewaltenteilung.body: State power is divided into three parts: {{Legislative}}, {{Exekutive}} and {{Judikative}}. Some questions use everyday words for them: {{Gesetzgebung}} (making laws), {{Regierung}} (government) and {{Rechtsprechung}} (judging). The three powers are separate so that nobody holds all the power. When a question asks what is **not** a power, three options are real and one is not.
gewaltenteilung.front: Name the three state powers in German.
gewaltenteilung.note: Only three. A fourth one is always wrong.

falle-vierte.text: A wrong option offers a fourth power: {{Direktive}} (directive) or {{Presse}} (the press). Germany has exactly three powers. {{Direktive}} only sounds like the three real words, and the {{Presse}} is free and not part of the state.

legislative.q: Which power do the Bundestag and the Bundesrat belong to?
legislative.body: The {{Bundestag}} and the {{Bundesrat}} belong to the {{Legislative}}: the power that makes the laws. In German this power is also called {{Gesetzgebung}}. Do not choose {{Exekutive}} or {{Judikative}}. They carry out and judge the laws, and they do not make them.
legislative.meaning: the legislative power, which makes laws
legislative.front: Which power makes the laws, and who belongs to it?
legislative.back: the legislative power: Bundestag and Bundesrat

exekutive.q: What belongs to the executive, and what does not?
exekutive.body: The {{Exekutive}} carries out the laws. It includes the government ({{Regierung}}), the ministries ({{Ministerien}}), the police ({{Polizei}}) and the tax office ({{Finanzamt}}). The courts ({{Gerichte}}) do **not** belong to it. They belong to the {{Judikative}}, because they judge by the law.
exekutive.meaning: the executive power, which carries out laws
exekutive.front: Which power do the courts belong to?

pressezensur.q: What does a democracy not have?
pressezensur.body: {{Zensur}} (censorship) means that the state controls and forbids what the press may publish. This is **not** a feature of a democracy. These are features: {{regelmäßige Wahlen}} (regular elections), {{Meinungsfreiheit}} (freedom of expression) and {{verschiedene Parteien}} (different parties). The reason: the people can only rule if they can speak and read freely and can choose between parties.
pressezensur.front: Which thing about the press does a democracy not allow?
pressezensur.note: Elections, free speech, many parties belong to democracy.

items.q: Why is the {{Bundestag}} not the source of state power?
items.a: All state power comes from the people. The people elect the {{Bundestag}}.

items.q: Name the three state powers in German.
items.a: {{Legislative}}, {{Exekutive}}, {{Judikative}}.

items.q: Which power do the courts belong to, and which do the {{Bundestag}} and the {{Bundesrat}} belong to?
items.a: Courts: {{Judikative}}. {{Bundestag}} and {{Bundesrat}}: {{Legislative}}.

items.q: Why is censorship not a feature of a democracy?
items.a: The people need free information and free speech to use their power.

rechtsstaat.title: The state under the law
rechtsstaat.big: In a {{Rechtsstaat}} the state must obey the law, and a democracy may ban a party that fights the constitution.

rechtsstaat.body: {{Recht}} means law, and {{Staat}} means state. In a {{Rechtsstaat}}, the state itself must obey the law. All residents ({{Einwohner}}) must obey it too, not only Germans. The courts do not make the laws: that is the task of the legislative power.
rechtsstaat.meaning: a state governed by the rule of law
rechtsstaat.front: What must the state do in a Rechtsstaat?
rechtsstaat.back: The state must obey the law.

falle-recht.text: {{Recht}} in {{Rechtsstaat}} means law. It does not mean that the state is always right ({{Der Staat hat Recht}}). It also does not mean that there are only right-wing parties ({{rechte Parteien}}).

keine-willkuer.q: What is not allowed in a democratic Rechtsstaat?
keine-willkuer.body: In a democratic {{Rechtsstaat}}, an arrest needs a reason, for example a crime. A private police force ({{Privatpolizei}}) that arrests people for no reason is the opposite. People may criticise the government, and citizens may demonstrate peacefully. This protects people from the state: in the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945, many were arrested without a court. The {{Grundgesetz}} of 1949 was the answer.
keine-willkuer.case: Someone commits a crime and is arrested: that is allowed. Someone is arrested for no reason: that is not.
keine-willkuer.front: May a private police arrest people for no reason in a Rechtsstaat?
keine-willkuer.back: No. An arrest needs a reason.
keine-willkuer.note: A crime is a reason. Criticism is not.

parteiverbot.q: What happens to a party that fights the constitution?
parteiverbot.body: A party that wants to build a dictatorship is {{verfassungswidrig}}: against the constitution ({{Verfassung}}). It is not {{tolerant}}, not {{gesetzestreu}} (law-abiding) and not {{rechtsstaatlich orientiert}}. A party that fights against the {{Verfassung}} can be banned ({{verboten}}). So a democracy can defend itself against its enemies. The {{Grundgesetz}} of 1949 gives democracy this protection, because of the dictatorship of 1933 to 1945.
parteiverbot.front: What makes a party unconstitutional and bannable?
parteiverbot.back: when it fights against the constitution
parteiverbot.note: Aim: dictatorship. Criticism alone is not enough.

falle-kritik.text: A wrong option says a party can be banned for criticism, an expensive election campaign or a new programme. These are normal in a democracy. Only fighting against the constitution leads to a ban.

steps: 1933 to 1945: the state was not bound by law
the state must obey the law
lehre-1933.caption: The Basic Law is the answer to the dictatorship: it binds the state to the law and lets democracy defend itself.

items.q: What does {{Rechtsstaat}} mean for the state?
items.a: The state must obey the law, like everybody else.

items.q: Why is a private police that arrests people for no reason not allowed?
items.a: An arrest needs a reason, and the state is bound by law. In 1933 to 1945 this was not so.

items.q: When can a party be banned in Germany?
items.a: When it fights against the {{Verfassung}}, for example when it wants a dictatorship.

items.q: Which time in history do the rules of the {{Grundgesetz}} on law and democracy answer?
items.a: The dictatorship of 1933 to 1945.

wahlgrundsaetze.title: Why we vote, and how
wahlgrundsaetze.big: Elections let the majority change the government, and in Germany they are free, equal and secret.

wechsel.q: What do regular elections make possible?
wechsel.body: Regular elections make a change of government possible. The majority of the voters decides who governs. The wrong options name other aims: forcing people to vote, keeping the old laws, or giving the poor more power. None of them is the function of elections.
wechsel.front: What do regular elections make possible?
wechsel.back: to make a change of government possible
wechsel.note: The majority of the voters decides.

recht.q: Is voting a duty or a right?
recht.body: Taking part in elections in Germany is a {{Recht}} (a right). It is not a {{Pflicht}} (a duty), not a {{Zwang}} (compulsion) and not a {{Last}} (burden). Every person decides alone whether to use this right.
recht.front: Is it your duty or your right to vote in Germany?
recht.note: Not a duty: you decide freely.

drei-grundsaetze.q: Which principles do elections in Germany follow?
drei-grundsaetze.body: Elections in Germany are {{frei}}, {{gleich}} and {{geheim}}. {{Frei}}: nobody may force or influence the voter. {{Gleich}}: every vote has the same weight, whatever the job or the sex of the voter. {{Geheim}}: nobody can see how you vote. Because the vote is secret, nobody can reward or punish a voter for the choice.
drei-grundsaetze.front: Which three words describe elections in Germany?
drei-grundsaetze.note: Secret: nobody can see your choice.

falle-grundsaetze.text: A wrong option is {{offen}} (open): the opposite of {{geheim}}. {{Sicher}} (safe) and {{geschlossen}} (closed) are not principles. {{Berufsbezogen}} and {{geschlechtsabhängig}} are the opposite of {{gleich}}.

frei.q: What does it mean that elections are free?
frei.body: In a free election the voter decides alone. Nobody may force or influence the voter. Every person decides whether to vote and whom to vote for. A voter must not suffer any disadvantage because of the election.
frei.front: What does it mean that elections are free?
frei.back: to decide without coercion whether to vote and whom to vote for
frei.note: No force, no influence, no disadvantage.

falle-frei.text: One wrong option plays with a phrase: {{frei geben}} means to give time off. This is not what free elections mean. Other wrong options say that voters may take money, that some people may not vote, or that everyone must vote.

meiste.body: The party that gets the most votes wins. Every vote counts the same, whoever casts it. So the votes of men, of women and of workers weigh the same. A wrong option names first votes for a chancellor candidate. That is a trap: voters do not choose the chancellor directly.
meiste.front: Which party wins an election in Germany?
meiste.back: the party with the most votes

mehrere-parteien.q: Why is there more than one party in a democracy?
mehrere-parteien.body: Citizens have different opinions. Different parties speak for these different opinions. So a democracy has more than one party: the different opinions of the citizens are represented. The wrong options name other aims. They are not the reason.
mehrere-parteien.front: Why does a democracy have several parties?
mehrere-parteien.back: because this way the different opinions of the citizens are represented

items.q: What do regular elections make possible?
items.a: A change of government, according to the will of the majority of the voters.

items.q: Is voting a duty in Germany, and how does that fit with free elections?
items.a: No. It is a right. In a free election each person decides alone whether to vote.

items.q: Name the three principles of elections in German.
items.a: {{frei}}, {{gleich}}, {{geheim}}: free, equal, secret.

items.q: Why does a democracy need more than one party?
items.a: Citizens have different opinions, and the parties represent them.

waehlen.title: Who may vote and how
waehlen.big: German citizens from 18 may vote in federal elections, at the polling station or by post, and election helpers count the votes.

alter.q: Who may vote in a federal election?
alter.body: In a federal election ({{Bundestagswahl}}) every person may vote who is a German citizen and at least 18 years old. Living in Germany is not enough, not even for 3 years or more. You must be a citizen. The wrong options for the age are 16, 21 and 23.
alter.case: After you become a German citizen, you may vote if you are at least 18 years old.
alter.front: Who may vote in a federal election?
alter.back: citizens of the Federal Republic of Germany who are at least 18
alter.note: Citizenship and age 18, not only living here.

aktives-wahlrecht.q: What is the active right to vote?
aktives-wahlrecht.body: {{Aktives Wahlrecht}} means: you can vote. If you are allowed to vote in a federal election, you have the {{aktives Wahlrecht}}. {{Wahl}} means election and {{Recht}} means right. To be elected is a different right, called {{passives Wahlrecht}}.
aktives-wahlrecht.front: What do we call the right to vote?
aktives-wahlrecht.note: Active: you can vote. Passive: you can be elected.

falle-wahlwoerter.text: Three wrong options also begin with {{Wahl}}: {{Wahlkampagne}}, {{Wahlkampf}} and {{Wahlverfahren}}. The first two are about the campaign before an election, the third is the procedure. Only {{Wahlrecht}} is the right to vote.

wahlbenachrichtigung.q: What do eligible voters receive before an election?
wahlbenachrichtigung.body: Before an election, citizens entitled to vote receive a {{Wahlbenachrichtigung}} from the municipality ({{Gemeinde}}). {{Wahl}} means election and {{Benachrichtigung}} means notification. The card tells you where your polling station ({{Wahllokal}}) is. The wrong options name the Federal President, the {{Bundesversammlung}} (Federal Assembly) and the parish office ({{Pfarramt}}). None of them sends the card.
wahlbenachrichtigung.front: Who sends the card before an election, and what is it called?
wahlbenachrichtigung.back: a polling card from the municipality

briefwahl.q: How can you vote without going to the polling station?
briefwahl.body: With {{Briefwahl}} you cast your vote by post. This is allowed in federal elections and in state elections. Each person votes alone: nobody may vote for another person, for example a wife. Voting by telephone is not allowed. Children from the age of 14 may not vote.
briefwahl.front: How can you vote without going to the polling station?

stimmzettel.q: What does a valid ballot paper look like?
stimmzettel.body: The ballot paper ({{Stimmzettel}}) of a federal election has two columns. You have 2 votes: one cross in the left column ({{Erststimme}}) and one cross in the right column ({{Zweitstimme}}). One cross shows one clear choice. More than one cross in a column does not, so that vote does not count. The two crosses may go to different parties.
stimmzettel.front: How many crosses do you make on a federal ballot paper?
stimmzettel.back: one cross in each column: first vote and second vote
stimmzettel.note: Two columns, one cross in each.

stimmzettel-bild.caption: Ballot 1 is valid: one cross in the left column ({{Erststimme}}) and one in the right column ({{Zweitstimme}}). Ballot 2 has two crosses in the right column. Ballots 3 and 4 have several crosses in the left column.

wahlhelfer.body: {{Wahlhelfer}} work at the polling station on election day. Their task is to count the votes after the election ends. Their work is an honorary office ({{Ehrenamt}}). The wrong options name other jobs: helping people to vote, writing cards and letters, and passing on interim results. These are not their task.
wahlhelfer.front: What is the task of election helpers?
wahlhelfer.back: They count the votes after the election ends.

ehrenamt.q: Which honorary office must German citizens accept?
ehrenamt.body: An {{Ehrenamt}} is an honorary office: a task for the community that people usually take on freely. One honorary office is a duty: German citizens must take on the {{Wahlhelfer}} office if they are asked. They may refuse only for an important reason. The wrong options are club coach, library supervisor and teacher.
ehrenamt.front: Which honorary office must a citizen accept if asked?
ehrenamt.note: The one honorary office that is a duty.

items.q: Who may vote in a federal election?
items.a: German citizens who are at least 18 years old.

items.q: What does {{aktives Wahlrecht}} mean?
items.a: It means that you can vote.

items.q: What do you receive before an election, and how can you vote without going there?
items.a: A {{Wahlbenachrichtigung}} from the municipality. You can vote by post: {{Briefwahl}}.

items.q: What do election helpers do, and what is special about their office?
items.a: They count the votes. It is the one honorary office that citizens must accept if asked.

bundestagswahl.title: Electing the Bundestag
bundestagswahl.big: The people elect the Bundestag, the parliament for Germany, every 4 years, but they do not elect the Federal President directly.

volk-waehlt.body: The people entitled to vote elect the members of the {{Bundestag}}. The military, business and the administration ({{Verwaltung}}) do not. The people elect the {{Bundestag}} directly. They do not elect the Chancellor, a minister-president or the Federal President directly.
volk-waehlt.front: Whom do the people elect in federal elections?
volk-waehlt.note: The people elect parliament, not the Chancellor.

wahlkette.caption: The people elect the Bundestag directly. They do not elect the Chancellor or the Federal President directly.

bundestagswahl.body: The {{Bundestagswahl}} is the election of the parliament for the whole of Germany. {{Bund}} is the federation, {{Tag}} is an assembly and {{Wahl}} is an election. It is not the election of the Chancellor or the Federal President. The parliaments of the states are elected in other elections.
bundestagswahl.front: What do voters elect in a Bundestagswahl?

landtagswahl.q: What is the election of a state parliament called?
landtagswahl.body: A {{Landtagswahl}} is the election of the parliament of a federal state. {{Land}} means state and {{Tag}} means assembly. The wrong options are {{Bundestagswahl}} (the federal parliament), {{Kommunalwahl}} (the local election) and {{Europawahl}} (the election of the European Parliament).
landtagswahl.front: What do we call the election of a state parliament?

wahlen-vergleich.title: Two elections, two parliaments
head: {{Bundestagswahl}}
{{Landtagswahl}}
rows: the parliament for the whole of Germany
the parliament of one federal state

vier-jahre.q: How often is the Bundestag elected?
vier-jahre.body: The {{Bundestag}} is elected for 4 years ({{vier Jahre}}). So federal elections normally take place every 4 years. The wrong options are 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 years. Remember: 4 years.
vier-jahre.front: For how long is the Bundestag elected?

abgeordnete.q: What are elected members of parliament called?
abgeordnete.body: Members of parliament who are elected by the citizens are called {{Abgeordnete}}. Members of the {{Bundestag}} are {{Bundestagsabgeordnete}}. Members of a state parliament are {{Landtagsabgeordnete}}. Chancellor, ambassador and minister-president are other jobs, not the name for elected members of parliament.
abgeordnete.front: What do we call members of parliament elected by the citizens?

bundespraesident.q: Whom can citizens not elect directly?
bundespraesident.body: Citizens do not elect the Federal President ({{Bundespräsident}}) directly. They elect the members of the {{Bundestag}}, of a state parliament ({{Landtag}}) and of the European Parliament directly.
bundespraesident.front: Which office do the voters not decide directly?
bundespraesident.note: Citizens elect parliaments, not the Federal President.

falle-personen.text: A wrong option names the Chancellor, the minister-president or the Federal President. The people do not elect any of these three directly.

items.q: Who elects the Bundestag, and for how many years?
items.a: The people entitled to vote elect it, for 4 years.

items.q: What is the difference between a {{Bundestagswahl}} and a {{Landtagswahl}}?
items.a: The {{Bundestagswahl}} elects the parliament for Germany. The {{Landtagswahl}} elects the parliament of one federal state.

items.q: What are elected members of parliament called?
items.a: {{Abgeordnete}}

items.q: Whom do the people not elect directly?
items.a: The Federal President. They do not elect the Chancellor or a minister-president directly either.

zweitstimme.title: The second vote and the 5% threshold
zweitstimme.big: A party needs 5% of the second votes to enter the Bundestag, and they decide how many seats it gets.

zweitstimme.q: What does the second vote decide?
zweitstimme.body: In a federal election you have two votes. With the second vote ({{Zweitstimme}}) you vote for a party. The more second votes a party gets, the more seats it gets in parliament. Direct candidates belong to the first vote ({{Erststimme}}), not to the second.
zweitstimme.front: What do the second votes decide in a federal election?
zweitstimme.back: how many seats a party gets in parliament

erst-zweit.title: The two votes
head: {{Erststimme}} (first vote)
{{Zweitstimme}} (second vote)
rows: which candidate is chosen directly in your constituency
how many seats a party gets

huerde.body: A party must get at least 5% of the second votes to enter the {{Bundestag}}. This minimum share of votes is called the {{5%-Hürde}}. A {{Hürde}} is a hurdle: a party must get over it. The wrong options are 3%, 4% and 6%.
huerde.front: What is the minimum share of votes for the Bundestag called, and how big is it?
huerde.back: the 5% threshold: at least 5% of the second votes

falle-huerde.text: The 5% threshold counts the votes of the voters in the election. It is not a rule inside the {{Bundestag}}: not a voting rule for small parties and not an {{Anwesenheitskontrolle}} (attendance check).

huerde-grund.body: Many small parties in the {{Bundestag}} make it harder to form a government ({{Regierungsbildung}}). The more parties must agree, the harder it is. The 5% threshold keeps very small parties out of the {{Bundestag}}. The wrong options name other reasons: similar programmes, lost orientation of citizens, and the money of small parties.
huerde-grund.front: Why does the Bundestag election have a minimum share of votes?
huerde-grund.back: because many small parties make it harder to form a government
huerde-grund.note: Fewer parties: easier to form a government.

wahlsystem.q: Which electoral system does Germany have?
wahlsystem.body: Germany's electoral system combines two systems. In {{Mehrheitswahlrecht}} (majority voting) the candidate with the most votes wins. In {{Verhältniswahlrecht}} (proportional representation) the seats are shared in proportion to the votes. The first vote works in the first way and the second vote in the second way.
wahlsystem.front: Which two systems does the German electoral system combine?
wahlsystem.note: First vote: majority. Second vote: proportional.

falle-wahlrechte.text: The wrong options are voting rights that are not equal: {{Zensuswahlrecht}} (by property), {{Dreiklassenwahlrecht}} (by class) and {{Männerwahlrecht}} (only men). Today every vote is equal ({{gleich}}).

items.q: What does the second vote decide?
items.a: How many seats a party gets in parliament.

items.q: What is the 5% threshold, and how many percent does a party need?
items.a: The {{5%-Hürde}} is the minimum share of the second votes to enter the Bundestag. A party needs at least 5%.

items.q: Why is there a 5% threshold?
items.a: Many small parties make it harder to form a government.

items.q: Which two systems does the German electoral system combine?
items.a: Majority voting and proportional representation: {{Mehrheits- und Verhältniswahlrecht}}.

parteien.title: Parties, groups and coalitions
parteien.big: Parties have abbreviations, their members form a group in parliament, parties can govern together, and citizens can form initiatives.

kuerzel.q: What do CDU, CSU, SPD and FDP stand for?
kuerzel.body: An abbreviation ({{Abkürzung}}) takes the first letter of each word. {{Christlich}} means Christian, {{demokratisch}} means democratic, {{sozial}} means social and {{frei}} means free. {{Union}} means union and {{Partei}} means party. The full names are in the table below.
kuerzel.front: What do the letters CDU, CSU, SPD and FDP stand for?
kuerzel.back: Christian Democratic Union, Christian Social Union, Social Democratic Party of Germany, Free Democratic Party
kuerzel.note: The D in CDU and FDP is Demokratische.

falle-kuerzel.text: In CDU and FDP the D is {{Demokratische}}, not {{Deutsche}} or {{Deutschland}}. In CSU the S is {{Soziale}}, not {{Süddeutsche}}. In SPD the first word is {{Sozialdemokratische}}, not {{Sozialistische}}.

fraktion.q: What is the group of one party's members in parliament called?
fraktion.body: The members of one party in parliament form a {{Fraktion}}. The wrong options are other words: {{Verband}} (association), {{Ältestenrat}} (Council of Elders) and {{Opposition}} (the parties that do not govern).
fraktion.front: What do we call the members of one party in parliament together?
fraktion.note: One party: Fraktion. Several parties in government: Koalition.

koalition.q: What is the cooperation of parties in a government called?
koalition.body: Often no single party has a majority in parliament. Then parties work together to form a government. This cooperation is called a {{Koalition}}. The wrong options are {{Einheit}} (unity), {{Ministerium}} (ministry) and {{Fraktion}}, the group of one party.
koalition.front: What do we call parties that work together to form a government?

ampel.body: The {{Ampelkoalition}} is a coalition of three parties: {{SPD}}, {{FDP}} and {{Bündnis 90/Die Grünen}}. {{Ampel}} means traffic light. The colours of the three parties are red (SPD), yellow (FDP) and green ({{Die Grünen}}), like the lights of a traffic light. Other combinations are not an {{Ampelkoalition}}.
ampel.back: SPD, FDP and Bündnis 90/Die Grünen in one government

groesste-fraktionen.q: Which are the two largest parliamentary groups in the Bundestag at present?
groesste-fraktionen.body: At present the two largest {{Fraktionen}} in the {{Bundestag}} are CDU/CSU and AfD. CDU and CSU are two parties. In the {{Bundestag}} they work together as one {{Fraktion}}. {{AfD}} stands for {{Alternative für Deutschland}}. This is the situation in 2025.
groesste-fraktionen.front: Which two parliamentary groups are the largest in the Bundestag at present?

buergerinitiative.q: What can citizens do to keep their bus route?
buergerinitiative.body: A {{Bürgerinitiative}} is a group of citizens who act together for a common goal. You can join an initiative or start one yourself. In this way citizens can take part in politics between elections. The other options (a sports club, the tax office, the forestry office) do not help to keep a bus route.
buergerinitiative.case: Your bus route to work is to be closed. You join an initiative for the route, or you start one.
buergerinitiative.front: What can citizens do together if they want to keep a bus route?
buergerinitiative.back: join a citizens' initiative or start one
buergerinitiative.note: Between elections, citizens can act too.

items.q: What does the D stand for in CDU and in FDP?
items.a: {{Demokratische}} (democratic).

items.q: What is the difference between a {{Fraktion}} and a {{Koalition}}?
items.a: A {{Fraktion}} is the members of one party in parliament. A {{Koalition}} is several parties governing together.

items.q: Which parties form the {{Ampelkoalition}}, and why is it called that?
items.a: SPD, FDP and Bündnis 90/Die Grünen. Their colours are red, yellow and green, like a traffic light ({{Ampel}}).

items.q: What can citizens do together to keep a bus route?
items.a: Join or start a {{Bürgerinitiative}}.

bundestag.title: The Bundestag and the opposition
bundestag.big: The Bundestag, elected by the people, passes the laws for all of Germany, and the opposition scrutinises the government.

bundestag.q: Which parliament passes the laws for the whole of Germany?
bundestag.body: The {{Parlament}} (parliament) for the whole of Germany is the {{Bundestag}}. {{Bund}} means federation. The {{Bundestag}} passes the laws ({{Gesetze}}). The government, the courts and the police do not pass laws.
bundestag.front: Which body is the parliament for all of Germany and passes the laws?
bundestag.note: Bund: federation. The Bundestag passes laws.

falle-bundes.text: Three wrong options sound right. The {{Bundesversammlung}} only elects the Federal President, and the {{Bundesgerichtshof}} is a court. The {{Volkskammer}} was the parliament of the GDR.

sitz.q: Where does the Bundestag meet, and what does the building look like?
sitz.body: The {{Bundestag}} meets in Berlin, in the {{Reichstagsgebäude}}. A glass dome ({{Kuppel}}) sits on its roof. The {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}} sits in Karlsruhe, not in Berlin. The {{Bundesrat}} and the {{Bundeskanzleramt}} are in Berlin too, but in other buildings.
sitz.front: Where does the Bundestag meet, and which feature marks the building?
sitz.back: in Berlin, in the Reichstag building, with a glass dome
sitz.note: Look for the glass dome on the roof.

reichstag.caption: The {{Reichstagsgebäude}} in Berlin with its glass dome: the seat of the {{Bundestag}}. This is the answer. The wrong options name other buildings.

praesident.q: Who is usually elected President of the Bundestag?
praesident.body: The {{Bundestag}} elects its own president ({{Bundestagspräsident}} or {{Bundestagspräsidentin}}). The president chairs the sessions. Usually the president comes from the largest {{Fraktion}}. A {{Fraktion}} (parliamentary group) is a group of members who work together, usually from one party.
praesident.front: From which group does the President of the Bundestag usually come?
praesident.note: Fraktion: members of parliament who work together.

aufgaben.q: Which tasks does the Bundestag have, and which one does it not have?
aufgaben.body: The {{Bundestag}} drafts and passes laws. It elects the Federal Chancellor. It scrutinises the federal government ({{Bundesregierung}}). It does **not** form the cabinet ({{Bundeskabinett}}), which is the chancellor and the federal ministers. The chancellor selects the ministers, and the Federal President appoints them.
aufgaben.front: Name tasks of the Bundestag and the one thing it does not do.
aufgaben.back: drafts laws, scrutinises the government; does not form the cabinet

falle-nicht.text: Three options are real tasks of the {{Bundestag}}: drafting laws, scrutinising the government and electing the chancellor. Only forming the cabinet is **not** one.

opposition.q: Who is the opposition, and what does it do?
opposition.body: The {{Opposition}} means all members of parliament who do not belong to the governing party or parties. The governing parties ({{Regierungsparteien}}) are the opposite. The opposition scrutinises ({{kontrolliert}}) the government. It does not select the ministers.
opposition.front: Who belongs to the opposition, and what is its task?
opposition.back: all members not in the governing parties; it scrutinises the government

mehrheit.q: What happens when members change their parliamentary group?
mehrheit.body: A government has a majority ({{Mehrheit}}) when the governing parties hold more than half of the seats. Each member decides by his or her own conscience. So members may change their {{Fraktion}}. The Federal President does not need to agree, and the voters do not vote again. But if members leave a governing group, the government can lose its majority.
mehrheit.front: What can follow when members of the Bundestag change their group?
mehrheit.back: The government can lose its majority.
mehrheit.note: Fewer seats for the governing parties.

items.q: Which body passes the laws for all of Germany, and where does it sit?
items.a: The {{Bundestag}}. It sits in Berlin, in a building with a glass dome.

items.q: Name three tasks of the {{Bundestag}} and one thing it does not do.
items.a: It drafts laws, elects the chancellor and scrutinises the government. It does not form the cabinet.

items.q: Who belongs to the opposition, and what does it do?
items.a: All members who are not in the governing parties. It scrutinises the government.

items.q: Why can a change of {{Fraktion}} cost the government its majority?
items.a: Then the governing parties may hold fewer than half of the seats.

regierung.title: Chancellor and Federal President
regierung.big: The chancellor, elected by the Bundestag, leads the government, and the Federal President, elected by the Federal Assembly, represents the country.

kanzler.q: Who elects the Federal Chancellor, and who chairs the cabinet?
kanzler.body: The {{Bundestag}} elects the Federal Chancellor ({{Bundeskanzler}} or {{Bundeskanzlerin}}). The chancellor chairs the cabinet ({{Bundeskabinett}}). The cabinet is the chancellor and the federal ministers together. The wrong options are the {{Bundesrat}}, the {{Bundesversammlung}}, the people and the {{Bundesregierung}}.
kanzler.front: Who elects the Federal Chancellor, and who chairs the cabinet?
kanzler.back: The Bundestag elects the chancellor. The chancellor chairs the cabinet.
kanzler.note: Bundestag: parliament. Cabinet: chancellor and ministers.

wahlkette.caption: The people elect the {{Bundestag}}, and the {{Bundestag}} elects the chancellor. The people do not vote for the chancellor directly.

kanzleramt.q: Where does the Federal Chancellor work most often?
kanzleramt.body: The Federal Chancellor works most often in Berlin. The Federal Chancellery ({{Bundeskanzleramt}}) and the {{Bundestag}} are there. Bonn was the seat of government earlier. Schloss Bellevue is the official residence of the Federal President. Schloss Meseberg is a guest house of the government.
kanzleramt.front: Where does the Federal Chancellor mostly work, and why there?
kanzleramt.back: in Berlin, because the Chancellery and the Bundestag are there
kanzleramt.note: Schloss Bellevue belongs to the President.

kanzler-name.q: Who is the current Federal Chancellor?
kanzler-name.body: Friedrich Merz is the Federal Chancellor. Gerhard Schröder and Angela Merkel were chancellors earlier. Ursula von der Leyen was never chancellor. The name can change when a new chancellor is elected.
kanzler-name.front: Who is the current Federal Chancellor?

staatsoberhaupt.q: Who is the head of state, and what is the main task?
staatsoberhaupt.body: The head of state ({{Staatsoberhaupt}}) of Germany is the Federal President ({{Bundespräsident}} or {{Bundespräsidentin}}). The main task is to represent the country ({{repräsentiert das Land}}). The President does not govern and does not draft laws. Governing is the task of the chancellor and the cabinet.
staatsoberhaupt.front: Who is the head of state, and what is the main task?
staatsoberhaupt.back: the Federal President; he or she represents the country

falle-praesident.text: Many wrong options name other presidents. The {{Bundestagspräsident}} chairs the Bundestag, and the {{Bundesratspräsident}} chairs the Bundesrat. Neither is head of state, and neither chairs the cabinet.

praesident-name.q: Who is Germany's head of state now?
praesident-name.body: Frank-Walter Steinmeier is the Federal President, so he is the head of state. Joachim Gauck was Federal President earlier. Bärbel Bas and Bodo Ramelow are not heads of state. The name can change when a new President is elected.
praesident-name.front: Who is Germany's current head of state?

ernennung.q: What does the Federal President do for the chancellor and the ministers?
ernennung.body: The Federal President proposes the chancellor to the Bundestag, and the Bundestag elects the chancellor. The President then appoints ({{ernennt}}) the elected chancellor. The chancellor selects the ministers, and the President appoints them. The President does not select them and does not run the government.
ernennung.case: In 1974 Federal President Gustav Heinemann gave Helmut Schmidt the certificate of appointment as chancellor.
ernennung.front: What does the Federal President do about the chancellor and the ministers?
ernennung.back: He or she proposes the chancellor for election and appoints the ministers.

ernennungsurkunde.caption: The photo from 1974: the Federal President gives the new chancellor, Helmut Schmidt, the certificate of appointment ({{Ernennungsurkunde}}). The answer to the question is another task: the President proposes the chancellor for election.

praesident-wahl.body: The {{Bundesversammlung}} (Federal Assembly) elects the Federal President. It meets only for this election. Its members are all members of the {{Bundestag}} plus the same number chosen by the state parliaments. The {{Bundestag}} alone, the {{Bundesrat}} and the {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}} do not elect the President.
praesident-wahl.front: Who elects the Federal President, and who sits there?
praesident-wahl.back: the Federal Assembly: Bundestag members plus members from the state parliaments

praesident-kanzler.title: Head of state and head of government
head: {{Bundespräsident}}
{{Bundeskanzler}}
rows: leads the government and chairs the cabinet

items.q: Who elects the chancellor, and who elects the Federal President?
items.a: The {{Bundestag}} elects the chancellor. The {{Bundesversammlung}} elects the Federal President.

items.q: Why is the President the head of state, but not the head of the government?
items.a: The President represents the country. The chancellor leads the government.

items.q: Who selects the ministers, and who appoints them?
items.a: The chancellor selects them. The Federal President appoints them.

items.q: What does the Federal President do before the {{Bundestag}} elects a chancellor?
items.a: The President proposes the chancellor for election.

bundesrat-gericht.title: Bundesrat, court, army and state tasks
bundesrat-gericht.big: The Bundesrat represents the federal states, the Federal Constitutional Court interprets the Basic Law, and the state has many tasks.

bundesrat.body: The {{Bundesrat}} represents the 16 federal states ({{Bundesländer}}) at the federal level. {{Rat}} means council. Its members are government representatives of the states ({{Regierungsvertreter der Bundesländer}}). Members of the {{Bundestag}}, federal ministers and party members do not sit there.
bundesrat.meaning: the council of the federal states
bundesrat.back: government representatives of the federal states

bundes-woerter.title: Four words that begin with {{Bundes}}
head: Who sits there
What it does
rows: passes laws, elects the chancellor, scrutinises the government
the states take part in federal law-making
the chancellor and the federal ministers
Bundestag members and the same number chosen by the state parliaments

verfassungsorgane.q: Which bodies are the constitutional bodies of Germany?
verfassungsorgane.body: {{Verfassung}} means constitution, and {{Organ}} means body. The constitutional bodies ({{Verfassungsorgane}}) are the highest bodies of the state. The {{Grundgesetz}} (Basic Law) sets them up. The five permanent ones are the {{Bundestag}}, the {{Bundesrat}}, the {{Bundespräsident}}, the {{Bundesregierung}} and the {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}}. A {{Bürgerversammlung}} (citizens' assembly) is not one.
verfassungsorgane.front: Name the five permanent constitutional bodies of Germany.
verfassungsorgane.back: Bundestag, Bundesrat, Federal President, federal government, Federal Constitutional Court

falle-buerger.text: The question says {{nicht}} (**not**): look for the odd one out. {{Bürgerversammlung}} sounds democratic, because {{Bürger}} means citizen. But the Basic Law names no such body.

verfassungsgericht.q: Which court interprets the Basic Law?
verfassungsgericht.body: The {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}} is responsible for interpreting the {{Grundgesetz}} (Basic Law). {{Auslegung}} (interpretation) means explaining what the text means. {{Verfassung}} means constitution, so the name tells you the job. The court sits in Karlsruhe.
verfassungsgericht.front: Which court interprets the Basic Law, and where does it sit?
verfassungsgericht.back: the Federal Constitutional Court, in Karlsruhe

falle-gericht.text: All four options end in {{gericht}} (court). {{Amtsgericht}} is a local court, {{Oberlandesgericht}} a higher regional court, and {{Verwaltungsgericht}} an administrative court. Only the name with {{Verfassung}} fits the Basic Law.

bundeswehr.body: The {{Bundeswehr}} is the German army ({{Armee}}). {{Bund}} means federation, and {{Wehr}} means defence. So the name says: the defence force of the federation. The police, a port and a citizens' initiative ({{Bürgerinitiative}}) are the wrong options.

staatsaufgaben.q: Which tasks does the German state have, and which does it not have?
staatsaufgaben.body: The state builds roads and schools. It pays child benefit ({{Kindergeld}}), supports museums and supports sportspeople. It does not sell food or clothing and does not produce cars and buses: companies do that. It does not supply all residents with free newspapers either. It does **not** pay for holiday trips for all nationals.
staatsaufgaben.front: Name one task of the German state and one thing it does not do.
staatsaufgaben.back: builds roads and schools; does not pay for holiday trips
staatsaufgaben.note: Child benefit and museums are tasks, too.

items.q: Who sits in the {{Bundesrat}}, and whom do they represent?
items.a: Government representatives of the federal states. They represent the 16 states.

items.q: Why is the {{Bundesverfassungsgericht}} the court for the Basic Law?
items.a: {{Verfassung}} means constitution. This court interprets the {{Grundgesetz}}.

items.q: What do the two parts of {{Bundeswehr}} mean?
items.a: {{Bund}} is the federation and {{Wehr}} is defence. It is the German army.

items.q: Name one task of the state and one thing it does not pay for.
items.a: It builds roads and schools. It does not pay for holiday trips.

ebenen.title: The three levels of the state
ebenen.big: Germany has three levels with their own tasks and leaders, and the states take part in federal law-making through the {{Bundesrat}}.

stufen.q: What are the three levels of the German state?
stufen.body: Germany has three levels. From top to bottom they are the {{Bund}} (federation), the {{Länder}} (states) and the {{Gemeinden}} (municipalities). The {{Gemeinde}}, also called {{Kommune}}, is the lowest political level. {{Stadträte}} (town councils), {{Landräte}} (district administrators) and {{Bezirksämter}} (district offices) are not levels. Occupation zones, an eastern and a western state belong to the past, and cantons belong to Switzerland.
stufen.front: Which three levels does the German state have?
stufen.back: Federation, states, municipalities. The municipality is the lowest level.
stufen.note: From top to bottom: Bund, Länder, Gemeinden.

bundeslaender.q: How many federal states does Germany have?
bundeslaender.body: Germany has 16 federal states ({{Bundesländer}}, short: {{Länder}}), not 14, 15 or 17. Nordrhein-Westfalen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Sachsen-Anhalt are real states with two-part names. Elsass-Lothringen (Alsace-Lorraine) is not a German state. The area lies in France.
bundeslaender.front: Into how many states is Germany divided?
bundeslaender.note: Elsass-Lothringen is not a German state.

karte.caption: The map shows the 16 states and their capitals. Find Nordrhein-Westfalen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Sachsen-Anhalt.

landesregierung.q: Which institution does every state have?
landesregierung.body: Every {{Bundesland}} has its own government, the {{Landesregierung}}. A state has no army, no currency and no foreign minister of its own. Foreign policy belongs to the federation, the {{Bund}}. That is why no state has a foreign minister.
landesregierung.front: What does every German state have of its own?
landesregierung.note: Foreign policy is federal, so no state has a foreign minister.

ministerpraesident.q: What is the head of a state government called?
ministerpraesident.body: In most states the head of government is called {{Ministerpräsidentin}} or {{Ministerpräsident}}. The word is made of {{Minister}} and {{Präsident}}. The {{Ministerpräsident}} leads the {{Landesregierung}}. Only the city-states Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg use other titles.
ministerpraesident.meaning: the head of a state government
ministerpraesident.front: What is the head of a state government usually called?
ministerpraesident.note: Premierminister and Erster Minister are titles of other countries.

falle-titel.text: {{Premierminister}} and {{Erster Minister}} are titles in other countries. {{Senator}} is a trap too: in Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg a {{Senator}} is a state minister, not the head.

schulpolitik.q: Which level is responsible for schools?
schulpolitik.body: School policy ({{Schulpolitik}}) is above all a task of the states. So the {{Bundesländer}} decide on schools, not the teachers, the universities or the family ministry. {{Verteidigungspolitik}} (defence policy) and {{Außenpolitik}} (foreign policy) belong to the federation. {{Wirtschaftspolitik}} (economic policy) is not above all a task of the states either.
schulpolitik.front: Which level is above all responsible for school policy?
schulpolitik.note: Foreign and defence policy: the federation.

bundesrat.q: How do the states influence federal politics?
bundesrat.body: The states take part in federal legislation ({{Gesetzgebung}}) through the {{Bundesrat}}. In the {{Bundesrat}} sit members of the state governments. For many laws the {{Bundesrat}} must agree. After a change of government in a state, the majority in the {{Bundesrat}} can change. Then governing at federal level can become **harder** ({{schwieriger}}).
bundesrat.meaning: the Federal Council, where the states take part
bundesrat.front: How do the states take part in federal law-making?
bundesrat.note: A new majority in the Bundesrat makes governing harder.

falle-bundesrat.text: A wrong option names the {{Bundestag}}, but a state election does not change the majority there. Other wrong options say {{leichter}} (easier). The answer is {{schwieriger}} together with {{Bundesrat}}.

buergermeister.body: A {{Bürgermeisterin}} or {{Bürgermeister}} is the head ({{Oberhaupt}}) of a {{Gemeinde}}. The {{Gemeinde}} is the lowest level: a town or a village. A mayor does not lead a school, a bank or a party.
buergermeister.note: The municipality is the lowest level.

bund-land-gemeinde.title: The three levels side by side
head: {{Bund}}
{{Land}}
{{Gemeinde}}
rows: top level, one for all of Germany

items.q: Name the three levels from top to bottom, in German.
items.a: {{Bund}}, {{Länder}}, {{Gemeinden}} (also called {{Kommunen}}).

items.q: Which policy do the states decide, and why does no state have a foreign minister?
items.a: The states decide {{Schulpolitik}}. Foreign policy ({{Außenpolitik}}) belongs to the federation, so no state has its own foreign minister.

items.q: Why can a change of government in a state make federal governing harder?
items.a: The state governments sit in the {{Bundesrat}}. A new majority there can make governing at federal level harder.

items.q: Who leads a state government, and who leads a municipality?
items.a: In most states the {{Ministerpräsident}}. In a municipality the {{Bürgermeister}}.

aemter.title: Offices and your rights
aemter.big: Each office has its own job, and you can object when an authority treats you badly or sends a wrong bill.

ordnungsamt.q: Which office belongs to the municipality?
ordnungsamt.body: The {{Ordnungsamt}} belongs to the municipal administration ({{Gemeindeverwaltung}}). {{Ordnung}} means order and {{Amt}} means office. The wrong options belong to other bodies. The {{Pfarramt}} belongs to a church, the {{Finanzamt}} to the state and the {{Auswärtiges Amt}} to the federation.
ordnungsamt.front: Name an office of the municipal administration.

einwohnermeldeamt.q: Where do you register when you move?
einwohnermeldeamt.body: When you move house, you must register ({{sich anmelden}}) at the {{Einwohnermeldeamt}}. The word is made of {{Einwohner}} (resident), {{melden}} (to report) and {{Amt}} (office). The {{Standesamt}} is for marriage, the {{Ordnungsamt}} for public order and the {{Gewerbeamt}} for trades and businesses.
einwohnermeldeamt.case: You move to a new town and register at the office of your new town.
einwohnermeldeamt.front: Which office do you go to after you move to a new town?

standesamt.q: Where do you go first if you want to marry?
standesamt.body: If you want to marry, go to the {{Standesamt}} (registry office) **first**. {{Stand}} here means civil status. The {{Standesamt}} records marriages, births and deaths. The {{Einwohnermeldeamt}}, the {{Ordnungsamt}} and the {{Agentur für Arbeit}} (employment agency) are not the place for it.
standesamt.front: Which office comes first before a wedding?
standesamt.note: Stand means civil status: marriage, birth, death.

wohin.title: Which office for what?
head: You go there to
Not the place to
rows: deal with public order in the municipality

beschwerde.q: What can you do if an official treats you badly?
beschwerde.body: A {{Behörde}} is a public authority, for example an office of a city. If your contact person there treats you badly, you can complain ({{sich beschweren}}) to the head of the authority. The head is the {{Behördenleiterin}} or {{Behördenleiter}}: {{Behörde}} plus {{Leiter}} (head). You do not have to accept bad treatment, and you must not threaten anyone.
beschwerde.front: Whom can you complain to about an official?
beschwerde.back: to the head of the authority

widerspruch.q: What do you do about an incorrect bill from an authority?
widerspruch.body: If an authority sends you an incorrect bill, you lodge an objection ({{Widerspruch einlegen}}) with that authority. A {{Widerspruch}} is a formal protest against a decision of an authority. Do not leave the bill lying, do not send it back and do not take it to the {{Finanzamt}}.
widerspruch.front: What do you do about a wrong bill from an authority?
widerspruch.back: lodge an objection with the authority
widerspruch.note: The objection goes to the authority that sent the bill.

items.q: Which office do you go to when you move, and which when you want to marry?
items.a: The {{Einwohnermeldeamt}} when you move. The {{Standesamt}} when you want to marry, and you go there first.

items.q: To which level do the {{Ordnungsamt}}, the {{Finanzamt}} and the {{Auswärtiges Amt}} belong?
items.a: {{Ordnungsamt}}: the municipality. {{Finanzamt}}: the state. {{Auswärtiges Amt}}: the federation.

items.q: What can you do if an official treats you badly?
items.a: Complain to the head of the authority ({{Behördenleiter}}).

items.q: What do you do about an incorrect bill from an authority?
items.a: Lodge an objection ({{Widerspruch}}) with that authority.

land.title: Your state: {state}
land.big: Every state has its own capital, parliament, government and symbols, but foreign policy belongs to the federation.

hauptstadt.q: What is the capital of the state?
hauptstadt.body: Every state has a capital, the {{Landeshauptstadt}}. The parliament and the government of the state sit there.
hauptstadt.front: {state}: what is the capital of the state?

city.body: Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen are city-states ({{Stadtstaat}}). In a city-state the city itself is a federal state. So it has no separate capital.
city.meaning: a city that is a federal state of its own
city.front: {state}: what kind of federal state is it?

lage.q: Where does the state lie in Germany?
lage.body: The question shows a map of Germany with four numbered states. Look for the shape of your state and for its neighbours.

lage-bild.caption: The picture of the question. Here {state} is number {answer}.

wappen.q: What does the coat of arms show?
wappen.meaning: the coat of arms of a state
wappen.front: {state}: what does the coat of arms show?

wappen-bild.caption: The four pictures of the question. The coat of arms of {state} is {answer}.

flagge.q: Which colours does the state flag have?
flagge.body: Every state has its own flag, the {{Landesflagge}}. Learn the colours in the order of the answer, from top to bottom.
flagge.front: {state}: which colours does the state flag have?

landtag.q: For how many years is the state parliament elected?
landtag.body: The people of a state elect the state parliament: the {{Landtag}} or {{Landesparlament}}. In 15 states this happens every 5 years. Only Bremen votes every 4 years.
landtag.front: {state}: for how many years is the state parliament elected?

regierungschef.q: What is the head of government called?
regierungschef.body: In 13 states the head of government is the {{Ministerpräsidentin}} or the {{Ministerpräsident}}. The three city-states use other titles: {{Regierender Bürgermeister}} in Berlin, {{Erster Bürgermeister}} in Hamburg, {{Präsident des Senats}} in Bremen.
regierungschef.front: {state}: what is the head of government called?

aussenminister.q: Which minister does no state have?
aussenminister.body: Foreign policy is a task of the federation, the {{Bund}}. That is why no state has a foreign minister. A state does have ministers for finance, justice and the interior.
aussenminister.front: {state}: which minister does the state not have, and why?
aussenminister.note: Foreign policy belongs to the federation.

city.body: Foreign policy is a task of the federation, the {{Bund}}. That is why no state has a minister or senator for foreign affairs. In a city-state the ministers are called {{Senatorin}} or {{Senator}}.

wahlalter.q: From what age may you vote in local elections?
wahlalter.body: Each state sets the voting age for its local elections, the {{Kommunalwahlen}}. In some states it is 16, in others 18. For the {{Bundestag}} it is 18 everywhere.
wahlalter.meaning: the election in a town, a district or a municipality
wahlalter.front: {state}: from what age may you vote in local elections?

bremen.q: From what age may you vote for the parliament of Bremen?
bremen.body: The state parliament of Bremen is called the {{Bürgerschaft}}. You may vote for it from the age of 16. For the {{Bundestag}} the voting age is 18 everywhere.
bremen.front: Bremen: from what age may you vote for the Bürgerschaft?

politische-bildung.q: Where can you find out about politics?
politische-bildung.body: Every state has an office that informs people about politics: the {{Landeszentrale für politische Bildung}}. It is there for everyone.
politische-bildung.meaning: the state office for civic education
politische-bildung.front: {state}: where can you find out about political topics?

sh.body: Most states have a {{Landeszentrale für politische Bildung}}, an office that informs people about politics. In Schleswig-Holstein this is the task of the {{Landesbeauftragte für politische Bildung}}.
sh.meaning: the state commissioner for civic education

kreis.q: Which district belongs to the state?
kreis.body: The question names four districts. Only one of them lies in your state. The other three belong to other states.
kreis.front: {state}: which district does the test name for this state?

items.q: Why does no state have a foreign minister?
items.a: Foreign policy is a task of the federation, the {{Bund}}.

items.q: Name the three city-states.
items.a: Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen.

items.q: Which parliament do the people of a state elect?
items.a: The state parliament: the {{Landtag}} or {{Landesparlament}}.

diktatur.title: The dictatorship, 1933 to 1945
diktatur.big: From 1933 to 1945 the National Socialists ruled Germany as a dictatorship, without free elections and with a policy of state racism.

zeitraum.q: When did the National Socialists rule Germany?
zeitraum.body: The National Socialists ({{Nationalsozialisten}}) ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945. Their leader was Adolf Hitler. That is 12 years: 1933 plus 12 is 1945. The wrong options shift the start or the end, for example 1932 to 1950 or 1949 to 1963.
zeitraum.front: In which years did the National Socialists rule Germany?

kanzler.q: When did Hitler come to power as Reich Chancellor?
kanzler.body: In 1933 Adolf Hitler became {{Reichskanzler}}, the head of the government. {{Kanzler}} means chancellor. {{Reich}} was the name of the German state at that time. The dictatorship began in the same year, 1933.
kanzler.front: In which year did Hitler become head of the German government?
kanzler.note: The same year the dictatorship began.

diktatur.q: What kind of state did the National Socialists set up?
diktatur.body: In 1933 the National Socialists set up a {{Diktatur}} (dictatorship). In a dictatorship one person or one party rules, and the people cannot choose freely. This state is called the {{Dritte Reich}} (Third Reich). It was not a {{Demokratie}}, a {{Monarchie}}, a {{Fürstentum}} or a {{Räterepublik}}.
diktatur.front: What kind of state was the Third Reich?
diktatur.note: One party rules. No free elections.

merkmale.q: What was missing in the dictatorship, and what existed?
merkmale.body: The dictatorship took away the freedoms of the people. There were no {{freie Wahlen}} (free elections). The state banned parties ({{Verbot von Parteien}}). It censored the press ({{Pressezensur}}), arrested people without a reason ({{willkürliche Verhaftungen}}) and persecuted Jews ({{Verfolgung von Juden}}).
merkmale.front: Name one thing that was missing in the dictatorship and one that existed.
merkmale.back: no free elections; the banning of parties
merkmale.note: Elections and press were not free.

fehlte.title: What the dictatorship took away
head: Missing
Instead
rows: {{freie Entfaltung der Persönlichkeit}}: free development of the personality
{{Schutz der Menschenwürde}}: protection of human dignity

falle-verneinung.text: One question asks what did **not** exist: the answer is free elections. Another asks what did exist: the answer is the party ban. Press censorship, arrests without reason and persecution of Jews all existed; press freedom and human dignity did not.

rassismus.q: What kind of policy marked the Nazi state?
rassismus.body: The Nazi state ({{NS-Staat}}) made racism its official policy: {{staatlicher Rassismus}}. The state itself treated people as unequal because of a supposed race.
